themes.definition: What providers and deployers are expected to do, under the Commission's guidelines on Article 5 and the Omnibus, so that their systems do not become prohibited practices, and how that is assessed case by case.
themes.what_is_set_out: The guidelines say operators 'should therefore take necessary measures to ensure that they do not place on the market, put into service or use' prohibited systems, with each operator in the value chain acting where it is 'best placed'; providers must consider reasonably foreseeable use and misuse before market entry, deployers 'remain responsible' for lawful use, and continuous compliance requires ongoing monitoring and updates. Whether a practice is prohibited 'will require a case-by-case assessment', drawing on considerations such as the severity and scale of harm, ethical principles of fairness, and 'a precautionary approach' under uncertainty; market surveillance authorities must investigate the facts of each case. Providers that take 'appropriate preventive and mitigating measures', such as visible disclosure, informing users of limitations and building in safeguards against hallucination, or safeguards in scoring systems, may keep incidental manipulation or false output outside the ban, and providers are 'expected to take effective and verifiable measures' against foreseeable misuse; a provider or deployer aware that its system discriminates may be treated as exploiting vulnerabilities. For crime-risk prediction, the exclusion applies only where the AI supports a human assessment 'based on objective and verifiable facts'; for emotion recognition permitted on medical or safety grounds, necessity must be assessed objectively and deployers 'must employ safeguards to avoid the screening of employees'. Compliance with high-risk duties (risk management, human oversight, FRIA) is presented as helping avoid prohibitions, and the Omnibus prohibits systems that generate non-consensual intimate imagery unless they have safeguards 'to reliably prevent' it and correct misuse.
themes.holders: Providers, deployers and other operators in the AI value chain; manufacturers of products embedding AI; providers of generative systems; providers of image and video generation systems (Omnibus); market surveillance authorities (case investigation); human assessors in law enforcement. Several passages name no assessor.
themes.binding: Article 5 is binding; the coders record that the guidelines call it 'fully applicable and mandatory', with enforcement by affected parties in national courts including interim injunctions. The measures themselves are interpretive ('should', 'expected', 'encouraged', 'could', 'may'); the consequence of not taking them is that the system may fall within a prohibition. The Omnibus condition is statutory: without safeguards, placing on the market is prohibited.
themes.checks: Trigger: case by case; before placing on the market (foreseeable misuse); during use (lawful conditions, ongoing monitoring). Compared against: the significant-harm considerations; the average member of a targeted group or specific individuals (coder note); objective and verifiable facts linked to criminal activity; the medical or safety purpose. Metric or threshold: none. Who: providers and deployers; market surveillance authorities in investigations. Result: practice prohibited or not; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: Those operators should therefore take necessary measures to ensure that they do not place on the market, put into service or use AI systems that could constitute prohibited practices under Article 5 AI Act.
The application of Article 5 AI Act will require a case-by-case assessment, which takes due account of the specific situation at issue in an individual case.

In this specific case, their human assessment should ensure that any AI prediction or assessment of the risk of a person committing a crime is based on objective and verifiable facts linked to a criminal activity.

the system does not have reasonable and adequate technical safety measures and other safeguards to reliably prevent that generation or manipulation, taking into account reasonably foreseeable misuse, and to correct observed or reported misuse

themes.definition: Transitional dates by which systems already in use or on the market must comply, including the specific deadline for high-risk systems used by public authorities.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers and deployers of high-risk systems 'intended to be used by public authorities' must take the necessary steps to comply with all the Regulation's requirements and obligations by 2 August 2030 'in any case', which the coders note applies even to systems placed on the market earlier and not significantly changed (Art. 111(2), restated unchanged in the Omnibus). Providers of GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027. All systems in scope of Art. 50 must comply on 2 August 2026 regardless of when they were placed on the market, while the Omnibus gives generative systems already on the market until 2 December 2026 for the Art. 50(2) marking duty. Text generated before 2 August 2026 but published on or after that date must be labelled; labelling of pre-existing deep fakes is only encouraged. The AI Act also encourages high-risk providers to comply voluntarily during the transitional period.
themes.holders: Providers and deployers of high-risk systems intended to be used by public authorities; providers of GPAI models; providers and deployers within Art. 50; deployers publishing text or possessing deep fakes.
themes.binding: Statutory deadlines; consequences not stated in the passages except that Art. 50 breaches are fineable (para 152). Early compliance and retroactive labelling are encouraged only.

quotes.location: Art. 1(39)(a), replacing AI Act Art. 111(2); p. 35
quotes.quote: In any case, the providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities shall take the necessary steps to comply with the requirements and obligations laid down in this Regulation by 2 August 2030.
This requires all in scope AI systems placed on the market or put into service in the Union to be compliant with that provision on that date
Providers of high-risk AI systems are encouraged to start to comply, on a voluntary basis, with the relevant obligations of this Regulation already during the transitional period.

themes.definition: The provider's written system of policies and procedures that ensures compliance, including the procedures and frequency for testing and validation, and its variants for public authorities and small firms.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers of high-risk systems must put in place a quality management system that ensures compliance (Art. 17), covering among other things design control, quality assurance, data management, post-market monitoring and 'examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after the development of the high-risk AI system, and the frequency with which they have to be carried out'. In the Annex VII route a notified body assesses the system against Art. 17. Public authorities that put high-risk systems into service for their own use 'may' fold these rules into a quality management system adopted at national or regional level (Recital 81). The Omnibus makes implementation proportionate to the size of the provider while requiring 'the degree of rigour and the level of protection required', and lets SMEs without partner or linked enterprises comply with some elements in a simplified way.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk systems; public authorities acting as providers of systems for their own use; SMEs and start-ups; notified bodies (assessment).
themes.binding: Statutory (Art. 17; breach via Art. 16(c) recorded as fineable under Art. 99(4)(a)); the public-authority and SME options are permissive ('may').
themes.checks: Trigger: before, during and after development, at a frequency the provider sets in its QMS. Compared against: not stated in these passages (the coder note points to Art. 9(8) metrics). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the provider; a notified body assesses the QMS against Art. 17 where Annex VII applies. Result: not stated.

quotes.quote: Providers of high-risk AI systems shall put a quality management system in place that ensures compliance with this Regulation.

Public authorities which put into service high-risk AI systems for their own use may adopt and implement the rules for the quality management system as part of the quality management system adopted at a national or regional level

quotes.location: Art. 1(11), replacing AI Act Art. 17(2); p. 19
quotes.quote: Providers shall, in any event, respect the degree of rigour and the level of protection required to ensure the compliance of their high-risk AI systems with this Regulation.

themes.definition: Duties that AI systems, and the information they give people, meet EU accessibility law, including the directive on public sector bodies' websites and apps.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers of high-risk systems must ensure compliance with Directive 2016/2102, which concerns public sector bodies' websites and mobile apps, and Directive 2019/882, and Recital 80 asks them to do so 'by design'. Under Article 50, information that people are dealing with AI must be provided 'in an accessible format for natural persons with disabilities', must take into account the characteristics of vulnerable groups such as children and the elderly, and providers and deployers must assess whether accessibility rules apply to them. JRC143539 recommends designing and deploying AI 'in ways that promote fairness, accessibility and equal treatment, including for marginalised and underserved communities'.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk systems; providers and deployers within Art. 50; public administrations (JRC143539, implied).
themes.binding: Statutory (Art. 16(l), fines via Art. 99(4)(a)); restated in non-binding Art. 50 guidelines; JRC recommendation.
themes.checks: Trigger: design stage, and before relying on Art. 50 disclosures. Compared against: the accessibility directives. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: provider or deployer. Result: not stated.

quotes.quote: ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with accessibility requirements in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882.
The information must also be provided in an accessible format for natural persons with disabilities, as specified in Article 50(5) and Recital 132 AI Act
AI solutions should therefore be designed and deployed in ways that promote fairness, accessibility and equal treatment, including for marginalised and underserved communities.

themes.theme: Scope boundaries: repurposed, dual-use, research and excluded uses
themes.definition: Delivery duties that arise at the edges of the AI Act's scope: systems moved from excluded to covered purposes, dual-use systems, research, large-scale EU IT systems, international cooperation frameworks and law-enforcement exemptions.
themes.what_is_set_out: An entity that uses a military, defence or national-security AI system for another purpose 'should ensure' it complies with the Act unless it already does, and the Commission's guidelines add that this 'has to be verified before such use'; providers of dual-use systems, such as a biometric system offered for both law enforcement and national security, should ensure compliance. Large-scale EU IT systems listed in Annex X must take AI Act requirements into account in their evaluations. The exclusion for international law-enforcement and judicial cooperation depends on the competent market surveillance authorities assessing whether cooperation frameworks or agreements include 'adequate safeguards' for fundamental rights (Recital 22, restated twice in the guidelines). Research excluded from the Act should still follow recognised ethical and professional standards, but real-world testing 'is not covered by that exclusion' from Art. 50, and the applicability of the Art. 50 law-enforcement exemption to a system with mixed uses 'should be assessed in light of the particular deployment'.
themes.holders: Entities repurposing excluded systems, which may be public bodies [inference]; providers of dual-use systems; unnamed evaluators of Annex X systems; market surveillance authorities for law enforcement and justice; those conducting research; providers and deployers testing in real-world conditions.
themes.binding: Mostly recitals and guidelines ('should', 'has to be verified'); Art. 111(1) is statutory. Consequence of missing safeguards in cooperation frameworks: the exclusion would not apply [inference, per coder note].
themes.checks: Trigger: before repurposed use; evaluations under the Annex X legal acts; reliance on the cooperation exclusion; each deployment for the Art. 50 exemption. Compared against: AI Act requirements; adequate safeguards for fundamental rights. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the using entity; market surveillance authorities. Result: not stated.

quotes.quote: the entity using the AI system for the other purposes should ensure compliance of the AI system with the AI Act, unless the system already complies with that act, which has to be verified before such use.
The requirements laid down in this Regulation shall be taken into account in the evaluation of each large-scale IT system established by the legal acts listed in Annex X
Testing in real world conditions (inside or outside of AI regulatory sandboxes) is not covered by that exclusion.

themes.theme: Procurement checks and due diligence on suppliers and third-party models
themes.definition: Checks a public body is expected to make on AI systems or models it buys or reuses from others, and the monitoring of its dependency on suppliers.
themes.what_is_set_out: EDPS guidance puts checks inside the procurement cycle: a risk evaluation 'before any budget is actually committed', mitigation devised for each phase, and, under the accountability principle, 'it is up to the controller to perform checks' at selection and award, followed by monitoring of implementation during contract execution. Buyers of pre-trained systems should understand the provider's development process, compare the demographics of training data with those of the data the system will process, and 'request from the provider a set of metrics' to evaluate the system against the organisation's objectives. For generative AI, EUIs should assess a third-party model's data-protection compliance and 'request all documentation to perform the verification', include data minimisation in assessments of third-party services, and verify that a model they deploy was not developed by unlawfully processing personal data; the EDPB likewise expects a controller deploying an acquired model to assess its lawful origin, for instance whether the data came from a breach or a finding of infringement. The Parliament requires AI Act compliance whether it develops or acquires AI and says 'Dependency on external experts or external service providers must be limited and monitored'. JRC129100 asks, as an open question, how ex ante impact assessment rules can be applied to solutions to be procured, and the AI Act records a provider's reliance on third-party pre-trained tools in its technical documentation.
themes.holders: EUIs and controllers procuring or deploying third-party AI; organisations procuring pre-trained systems; the Parliament's administration; controllers deploying acquired models (EDPB); providers (Annex IV record of third-party tools).
themes.binding: EDPS and EDPB restate accountability duties in non-binding guidance ('should', 'it is up to the controller', 'would need to'); EDPS cites the Financial Regulation's execution step as a statutory procurement duty (coder field); EP2024 'shall' and 'must' in an internal framework; JRC poses a question.
themes.checks: Trigger: procurement (call for tenders, selection, award, before budget is committed); before deploying an acquired model [inference]; contract execution. Compared against: the organisation's objectives; the concerns listed in EDPS sections 4-5; data-protection requirements; the demographics of operational data. Metric or threshold: metrics supplied by the provider (the coder note lists fairness metrics such as false positive and false negative rate parity); no thresholds. Who: the controller or EUI. Result: not stated.

quotes.location: p.11, s.3.3 Procuring an AI system
quotes.quote: it is also important to acknowledge , already in the procurement cycle , making a risk evaluation before any budget is actually committed for a solution that would bring undesirable risks to the organisation.
the organisation should request from the provider a set of metrics that will allow for the evaluation of the AI system against the organisation’s objectives.

In case EUIs use a generative AI model developed by another entity, they should thoroughly assess and ensure that the generative AI complies with all data protection requirements, and request all documentation to perform the verification.
Dependency on external experts or external service providers must be limited and monitored.

themes.theme: Personal data protection in AI development and use
themes.definition: Data-protection duties applied to AI by the EDPS, the EDPB and the AI Act: minimisation, lawful basis, anonymity of models, rights requests, and the handling of personal data in training data, prompts and outputs.
themes.what_is_set_out: EU institutions must apply data-protection principles to AI: limit personal data to what is necessary, 'verify that the purpose in question cannot be achieved by processing other data, such as synthetic or anonymised data' before deciding to process personal data, prefer anonymised or pseudonymised data, validate the relevance of planned data types before full training, put safeguards on web scraping, and comply with Regulation 2018/1725 (restated by the Parliament for systems it considers using). The EDPB opinion sets how supervisory authorities should judge controllers: whether a model is truly anonymous, assessed with 'all the means reasonably likely to be used'; what tests and document-based audits the controller ran; whether the three cumulative conditions for legitimate interest are met, including a balancing test; and whether mitigation such as excluding objecting websites or 'output filters' to prevent regurgitation is in place. EDPS guidance addresses rights requests: identify whether personal data is in training data and whether the model 'might leak that data' when prompted, keep metadata for traceability, and use output filtering where unlearning is not viable; its generative AI orientations ask EUIs to work out whether a request concerns training data, fine-tuning data, user prompts or outputs, and to test that retrieval-augmented systems do not leak personal data. The Omnibus permits exceptional processing of special categories for bias detection, AI Act sandbox rules require isolated data environments, marking and detection must not process creators' data unnecessarily, and the Code commits signatories to zero retention of content uploaded for detection.
themes.holders: EUIs and data controllers; developers and deployers; supervisory authorities (as assessors under EU074); providers and deployers (Omnibus Art. 4a); prospective providers in sandboxes; providers of marking and detection solutions and Code signatories; operators of the EU public-sector data space (JRC129100); Parliament's administration (implied).
themes.binding: Statutory duties under GDPR and EUDPR restated in guidance ('must', 'requires'); the EDPB opinion and EDPS guidance are otherwise non-binding ('should', 'possible measure', 'may'); Omnibus permissions are statutory with mandatory conditions; Code commitments bind signatories. The only consequence stated (EDPB) is that a supervisory authority may find a failure of accountability if it cannot confirm that a model was effectively anonymised.
themes.checks: Trigger: before processing (necessity check); during development (anonymity tests and audits); on a rights request; regular monitoring that no personal data is processed where not intended; when using retrieval-augmented generation. Compared against: necessity for the purpose; a likelihood of identification that is 'insignificant' (coder note); widely known state-of-the-art attacks; the three legitimate-interest conditions. Metric or threshold: likelihood of identification insignificant; otherwise none. Who: the controller; supervisory authorities evaluate. Result: processing judged not necessary; model not anonymous so data-protection law applies; corrective powers of supervisory authorities (coder note); otherwise not stated.

quotes.location: PDF p.25 (printed p.24), s.9 Data minimisation
quotes.quote: EUIs must also verify that the purpose in question cannot be achieved by processing other data, such as synthetic or anonymised data before deciding that personal data is necessary to process in the first place
SAs should take into consideration the scope, frequency, quantity and quality of tests that the controller has conducted on the model.

When machine un-learning is not viable, output filtering can be used. Output filtering involves real- time scanning of AI model responses to detect and block personal information before reaching users.

quotes.location: Art. 1(6), inserting AI Act Art. 4a(1); p. 17
quotes.quote: providers of such systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data, subject to appropriate safeguards for the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons.

themes.theme: Public value, needs, readiness and sustainability assessment
themes.definition: Recommendations that public administrations assess whether AI meets a real need, delivers public value and is affordable and sustainable, and that they evaluate its impact, before and after adoption.
themes.what_is_set_out: The two JRC reports recommend that public administrations assess needs 'with a focus on public value creation', trustworthiness and people-centric design, take stock of their readiness across technological, organisational and contextual factors before committing to any AI initiative, check that technological components are in place and of sufficient quality, and 'assess environmental, social and economic sustainability across the life cycle' of solutions they are considering. They call for generic but adaptable impact-assessment frameworks, covering a technical dimension (standards, robustness, life expectancy, cost, service level agreements, external sourcing) and a functional one such as public trust, for systematic measurement of the impact of AI-enabled public solutions, for quantifying environmental impacts across the AI value chain, for certification and labelling against sustainability principles, and for public administrations to ensure their own AI use does not cause environmental damage. JRC129100 presupposes that public bodies evaluate their AI systems against intended goals, unintended effects and negative consequences, but says they 'need to be assisted' to do so, and asks how ex ante impact assessment can apply to procurement. The Court of Auditors applies the idea inside an institution: its AI projects follow the usual project-management process with 'performance indicators and cost-benefit analysis'.
themes.holders: Public administrations and agencies; stakeholders adapting impact frameworks; the ECA for its own projects. Many passages name no holder.
themes.binding: Recommendations and suggestions ('should', 'might want to', 'could', 'it is time'); the ECA item is an internal process requirement. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: before committing to an AI initiative; across the life cycle; ex ante for procurement; systematic ongoing measurement. Compared against: intended goals and public value; enabling factors; expected benefits against environmental and societal costs; sustainability principles aligned with EU environmental policy. Metric or threshold: key performance indicators, performance indicators and cost-benefit analysis, none specified. Who: public administrations; ECA project teams. Result: not stated, beyond deciding on adoption [inference].

quotes.quote: Public administrations should assess environmental, social and economic sustainability across the life cycle of the AI solutions they are considering.

Public bodies and agencies need to be assisted when evaluating their AI systems, whether to assess the achievement of intended goals, to gauge encountered uni ntended effects, or to take stock of potential negative consequences.
dedicated projects will follow the usual ECA project-management process, which includes performance indicators and cost-benefit analysis.

themes.theme: Security against AI-enabled threats and use of AI in cyber defence
themes.definition: ENISA recommendations on securing organisations' own AI tools and agents and on using AI in security operations, including human review of AI-generated fixes and triage.
themes.what_is_set_out: ENISA's paper on frontier AI asks every organisation to analyse its exposure to frontier AI, to secure 'agentic endpoints and enterprise browsers' as new attack surfaces, to assume adversaries may already be inside through the AI and software supply chain, and to build security into development rather than rely on oversight. It recommends using AI models for continuous red teaming and structured threat modelling, AI-assisted triage 'while keeping human review firmly in the loop', and frameworks for 'AI-enabled security tools that prioritise human oversight, auditability, and human-gated triage for decision making'; national authorities should run AI-powered threat hunting. It flags that verifying AI-generated code patches 'may become a major bottleneck' and that the challenge is to keep 'the human in the middle'. Model developers should train models to be 'structurally constrained' and suggest secure code. Several items concern defence against attackers' use of AI rather than governance of a public body's own tools, notably the target of single-digit-minute mean time to detect and respond.
themes.holders: Defenders and every organisation; national authorities; service providers; developers of AI models; technical teams and system managers. Several items name no holder.
themes.binding: Non-binding recommendations and analysis; no consequences ('n/a' in the coder fields).
themes.checks: Trigger: continuous or real-time; early and continuous threat modelling; incident triage; before deploying AI-generated patches [inference]. Compared against: absence of new vulnerabilities or bugs; live architectures. Metric or threshold: single-digit-minute mean time to detect and to respond; 24-hour notifications. Who: defenders, system managers, technical teams. Result: not stated.

quotes.location: page 11, Security fundamentals matter more than e…
quotes.quote: verifying these AI-generated patches may become a major bottleneck. System managers may face challenges to build tools that can quickly check and approve these fixes without accidentally introducing new bugs into the code.
using AI-assisted triage for real-time telemetry validation, prioritisation, and blast-radius containment, while keeping human review firmly in the loop to reliably hit 24-hour notifications.
AI-enabled security tools that prioritise human oversight, auditability, and human-gated triage for decision making.

themes.theme: General duties to comply with law and principles across the lifecycle
themes.definition: Umbrella requirements to ensure that an AI system complies with the AI Act, other law or stated principles, without setting out a specific procedure.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act makes providers 'ensure that their high-risk AI systems are compliant with the requirements set out in Section 2' (Art. 16(a)) and requires systems to comply in light of their intended purpose and the state of the art (Art. 8), and the Commission's guidelines restate that providers must ensure requirements are met before market entry; Recital 165 encourages voluntary additional requirements such as the Ethics Guidelines and AI literacy. EU institutions write similar duties for themselves: the Parliament requires legal and fundamental-rights requirements to be considered 'at all stages of an AI solution lifecycle, from scouting to ideation, from testing to deployment and ultimately to decommissioning', a 'robust and transparent compliance process', compliance with the law, and that AI 'must not threaten the dignity, integrity, liberty, privacy, safety and security' of people, and frames responsible use as a set of questions (for example 'Do we have regulatory compliance built in our workflows?'); the Court of Auditors 'will ensure that all AI tools and processes deployed at the ECA comply' with the AI Act. JRC documents tell public administrations to consider government use 'from an administrative law perspective', to make sure EU ethical, legal and administrative principles are followed, and to take the HLEG principles and three anchoring elements into account from the outset. These duties name outcomes, not methods.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk systems (AI Act); providers and deployers (voluntary, Recital 165); the Parliament's administration (often unnamed); the ECA; government and public administrations (JRC).
themes.binding: Statutory for providers (Arts 8 and 16(a); fines via Art. 99(4)(a)); Commission guidelines interpretive; internal requirements, imperatives, questions and commitments for EU institutions with no consequences; JRC recommendations; voluntary encouragement.
themes.checks: n/a (no procedure is set); where stated, the trigger is every lifecycle stage and the comparator is the law or principles named.

quotes.quote: ensure that their high-risk AI systems are compliant with the requirements set out in Section 2

Legal and fundamental rights requirements must be taken into account at all stages of an AI solution lifecycle, from scouting to ideation, from testing to deployment and ultimately to decommissioning.
We will ensure that all AI tools and processes deployed at the ECA comply with the requirements of the EU AI Act and other relevant EU legislation.

when planning, piloting or using AI-enabled technologies, public administrations should make sure that ethical, legal and administrative principles identified at the EU level are followed, and that deployed AI -based solutions are aligned with such values

not_themed.reason: Outside the object: a private bank's legally required anti-money-laundering crime-risk screening, not an AI tool used in the public sector or in public services; coder A flagged it as a scope doubt. Its content (human assessment and verification of predictions) is covered by the human-review theme through the law-enforcement passages EU-DEL-DES-180 and 181.

Off-topic: national authorities' proactive scanning of critical infrastructure as a defence against attackers' use of AI; the coder note says no AI tool of the authority is involved, so there is nothing about governing an AI tool.

absences: Every Delivery starting code has passages here: testing, evaluation, validation, monitoring, logging, recording, human review of outputs and impact assessment. What a reader would expect but does not find: (1) No numerical threshold for accuracy, error or performance of any public-sector AI tool. The AI Act requires testing 'against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds' and an 'appropriate level of accuracy' but leaves both to the provider; the only numbers in the cell are the six-month log retention, the 30% error margin for GPAI compute estimates, ENISA's security-operations targets and the Code's error-rate metric, which has no value. (2) Nothing on consistency or repeatability of outputs, that is, whether the same input gives the same result; Art. 15's 'perform consistently' and Recital 74 concern stability over the lifecycle [inference]. (3) Prompts and configuration are almost absent: only the ECA's optional 'quality controls and documentation' for a translation prompt library, plus data-protection references to prompts (rights requests covering user prompts, leakage 'when answering certain prompts', controls against prompt injection). (4) Model versions: change triggers exist (substantial modification, change of intended purpose, change of operating system or architecture, validation of a retrained version), but no passage requires a deployer to record which model or version produced a given output. (5) Confidence scores: only the 'probabilistic thresholds' of Art. 9(8), the 'threshold used' that national law may regulate for biometric identification, and an EDPS example of reading a probability score as a definitive diagnosis; no rule says which scores or cases are routed to a human. (6) Which cases reach a human is specified only for biometric identifications (all of them), crime-risk predictions, AI-generated public-interest text relying on the review exception, and ECA recruitment screening; there is no general rule for public-sector decisions in this cell. (7) The person or unit inside a public body that carries out deployer checks is rarely named; many AI Act articles and most EDPS measures are in the passive voice. (8) No independent check of a public deployer's own testing or monitoring: for Annex III points 2-8 conformity is self-assessed by the provider, and the deployer's monitoring standard is the provider's instructions. (9) Decommissioning is mentioned once (EP2020), with no procedure.
cross_cutting: This cell is dominated by the AI Act and the Commission and Omnibus texts that implement it, which put most delivery work on providers before market entry: conformity assessment (mostly self-assessment), risk management, data governance, testing against metrics the provider chooses, technical documentation, logging and post-market monitoring; the Article 50 guidelines and the Code of practice add a large, detailed block on disclosure, marking and labelling. Duties that fall on public bodies as users are thinner and scattered: the Art. 26 deployer duties (use as instructed, monitor against the instructions, check input data, keep logs), the Art. 27 fundamental rights impact assessment for bodies governed by public law, the 2 August 2030 deadline for high-risk systems used by public authorities, the market surveillance authority acting as notified body for law enforcement, migration and EU-institution systems, and labelling of AI-generated text on public administration and services. Most of the material on what a public user should actually check comes from EU institutions' own frameworks (Parliament, Commission, Court of Auditors, Commission staff rules) and from EDPS and EDPB guidance, written as commitments, 'should' and 'possible measures'; only the Parliament's 2024 framework names a consequence (suspension of the AI project). Binding force therefore runs from statutory duties with fines (provider and deployer duties, though the coders note that the FRIA is not fineable under Art. 99(4)) through interpretive guidelines and Code commitments to recommendations (JRC, ENISA), and holders are often unnamed. On checking AI outputs, the documents name categories (accuracy, robustness, bias, statistical accuracy, detection error rate) but set no thresholds, and leave metrics to providers; human review of individual outputs is set out in detail only for biometric identifications (two-person verification), Article 50 editorial review with fact-checking, and a few EU-institution rules (Commission staff to 'always critically assess' outputs, ECA recruitment and audit). Run-to-run consistency, prompts, model versions and confidence-score routing are essentially absent as objects of control.
authorship_note: Theme names, definitions, groupings, summaries and the absences and cross-cutting text are the analyst's (Claude's) synthesis of the coded passages, built on the framework and starting codes set in THEMATIC_INSTRUCTIONS.md. Quotes, locations, holders and the obligation and consequence details are taken from the coders' input lines; items marked [inference] are the analyst's or the coders' inferences, not text from the documents.
